BUSS1020 Week 05

BUSS1020 Week 05 - Continuous Distributions: Density, Normal, Uniform and Exponential

Overview

This week moves from discrete counts to continuous quantities:

• Continuous random variables and probability density functions (PDFs), and why a density height is not a probability.

• The normal (Gaussian) distribution: shape, parameters and the Empirical Rule.

• The standard normal distribution and the z transformation.

• The two directions of normal calculations: finding a probability from a value, and finding a value from a probability.

• How to assess whether data are approximately normal.

• The uniform distribution.

• The exponential distribution for waiting times, and its pairing with the Poisson distribution.

Key Concepts

Continuous random variables and probability density

A continuous random variable can take any value in an interval, for example waiting times, stock returns, weights, delivery times, coffee temperature, income or profit.

A probability density function (PDF), or density curve, is built from data as follows:

Collect observations, such as service times of 3.25, 3.687, 4.231 minutes.

Group them into classes (0-1, 1-2, 2-3 minutes, ...) and give each bar a density height of count divided by (total count x class width). For a one-minute-wide class containing 5 of 100 observations, the height is 0.05 per minute.

Each bar area equals its relative frequency, so the total area of all bars is 1.

A nonnegative smooth estimate with total area 1 can approximate the PDF. A theoretical PDF may instead be specified directly by a probability model.

Three rules for continuous distributions:

• P(X = x) = 0 for any single value: the area above one point is zero. Asking "what is the probability the wait is exactly 2.78653 minutes" has answer 0, so continuous probabilities are always asked for intervals.

• The total area under the density curve is 1.

• P(A < X < B) is the area under the curve between A and B: probability equals area.

Density height is not probability. The height f(x) shows where values are relatively more likely ("where the action is"); only the area under the curve over a range is a probability.

The normal distribution

• The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the symmetric, bell-shaped density. Its mean, median and mode all coincide at the centre.

• It has two parameters: mu (the location, or centre of the bell) and sigma (the spread). The theoretical range is minus infinity to plus infinity.

• Moving mu shifts the whole curve sideways without changing its shape. Increasing sigma makes the curve shorter and wider, so larger sigma means more spread and a lower peak.

• The Empirical Rule for normal data: about 68% of the probability lies within mu plus or minus 1 sigma, about 95% within 2 sigma, and about 99.7% within 3 sigma. Values beyond 3 standard deviations are extreme values, extremely unlikely under a normal model.

• Most real data are not exactly normal: the normal distribution is a model and an approximation. It arises naturally for sums of many random variables, for IQ scores, and for positions of particles in a fluid. It can fail badly in other settings, for example stock returns during a financial crisis, when extreme moves cluster together. Assuming normality is a modelling decision with real consequences.

The standard normal and the z transformation

• The standard normal distribution is the normal with mu = 0 and sigma = 1, written Z ~ N(0, 1). By symmetry, half of its probability lies above 0 and half below, so z-scores can be positive or negative.

• The z transformation is Z = (X - mu)/sigma. Subtracting mu moves the centre to 0; dividing by sigma puts the spread on a unit scale. The shape of the distribution does not change, only the location and the scale.

• The reverse transformation is X = mu + Z sigma.

Solving normal problems in the two directions

Type

Situation

Method

A: left tail

P(X < x)

NORM.DIST(x, mu, sigma, TRUE), or first z = (x - mu)/sigma and then NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE)

A: right tail

P(X > x)

1 minus the left-tail probability, because the total area is 1

A: interval

P(a < X < b)

P(X < b) - P(X < a); the mean splits the area 0.5 / 0.5, which often simplifies the arithmetic

A: up to the mean

P(a < X < mu)

0.5 - P(X < a)

B: reverse

given a probability, find x

Find z first with NORM.S.INV(p), then X = mu + Z sigma; or in one step NORM.INV(p, mu, sigma)

• Direction rule: when mu and sigma are given and a probability is wanted, go straight to NORM.DIST(x, mu, sigma, TRUE) and there is no need to convert to z. When a probability is given and x is wanted, solve on the z scale first and then transform back, because printed normal tables only cover the standard normal; software shortcuts it in one step.

• The fourth argument of NORM.DIST is TRUE for the cumulative probability (all probability up to the point).

• In a reverse problem, a probability below 50% must give a negative z (it lies below the mean), and a probability above 50% a positive z.

Assessing normality

Seven checks decide whether a data set can be treated as approximately normal:

The sample mean is close to the sample median.

The Empirical Rule roughly holds: about 68% of values within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2, 99.7% within 3.

The interquartile range is about 1.33 times the standard deviation (IQR = approximately 1.33 s).

The boxplot and the histogram look roughly symmetric and bell-shaped.

There are no obvious extreme or outlying observations.

The skewness is close to 0.

The excess kurtosis is close to 0 (excess kurtosis = kurtosis - 3, and the normal distribution has kurtosis 3).

No real data set is perfectly normal; the question is always whether the normal distribution is a reasonable approximation. The practical point of the checks is to decide whether to analyze the raw data directly or to work with a normal model.

The uniform distribution

• The uniform (rectangular) distribution has a constant density over an interval: f(x) = 1/(B - A) for A <= x <= B, and 0 outside.

• Why the height is 1/(B - A): the total area must be 1, so (B - A) times the height equals 1, giving height = 1/(B - A).

• Mean: mu = (A + B)/2. Standard deviation: sigma = (B - A) divided by the square root of 12.

• Interval probability: P(C < X < D) = (D - C) times 1/(B - A), which is just the area of the rectangle between C and D.

• Because the density is flat, all subintervals of equal length are equally likely. This is the opposite of the exponential distribution, whose density is highest near 0 and falls away.

The exponential distribution

• The exponential distribution models the waiting time between two events: gaps between diners arriving at a restaurant, between trucks arriving at a loading dock, between ATM transactions, or between trades in an asset. If customers arrive at 2 per hour, the average wait is 30 minutes.

• Division of labour with the Poisson distribution: the Poisson counts events in a fixed interval (a discrete random variable), while the exponential measures the time between events (a continuous random variable).

• Density: f(x) = lambda times e raised to the power (-lambda x), for x >= 0 and lambda > 0.

• Cumulative probability: F(x) = P(X <= x) = 1 - e raised to the power (-lambda x).

• Mean and standard deviation: mu = 1/lambda and sigma = 1/lambda, so the mean equals the standard deviation. The mode is 0 (the density is highest at x = 0), and the distribution is right-skewed, so mode < median < mean.

• Contrast to remember: exponential has mu = sigma; Poisson has mu = sigma squared.

• Lambda is the only parameter and it is a rate: lambda = 0.5 gives a mean wait of 2 units; lambda = 1 gives 1; lambda = 1.5 gives 0.667. A higher rate means shorter waiting times.

• Integral notation: P(X < x) is the integral from 0 to x of lambda e^(-lambda u) du. The symbol u is a dummy variable of integration; do not confuse it with the upper limit x.

The Poisson-exponential pairing requires a homogeneous Poisson process: independent counts in disjoint intervals, with a constant rate lambda per unit time. Then the time T between events is exponential with mean 1/lambda:

P(T > t) is the probability that no event occurs in the interval from 0 to t.

The number of events in that interval is Poisson with mean lambda t, so P(no events) = (lambda t)^0 e^(-lambda t) / 0! = e^(-lambda t).

Therefore P(T > t) = e^(-lambda t) and P(T < t) = 1 - e^(-lambda t), which is exactly the exponential cumulative function.

Intuition: if 6 events are expected in 60 minutes, the average gap is 60/6 = 10 minutes = 1/lambda. The average is only the centre of a distribution: individual gaps may be 12 minutes or 15 minutes. An expected average must not be confused with certainty about a random quantity.

Excel for continuous distributions

• NORM.DIST(x, mu, sigma, TRUE) gives P(X <= x). NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE) gives the standard normal cumulative probability. NORM.S.INV(p) gives the z for a left-tail probability p. NORM.INV(p, mu, sigma) gives the value x directly. NORM.INV(p, 0, 1) is the same as NORM.S.INV(p).

• NORM.DIST(x, mu, sigma, FALSE) returns the density height f(x), not a probability; a continuous variable has zero probability at any single point.

• Interval probability with a <= b: NORM.DIST(b, mu, sigma, TRUE) - NORM.DIST(a, mu, sigma, TRUE). Probability outside both bounds: CDF(a) + 1 - CDF(b). Keep the bounds in the right order and no absolute-value workaround is needed.

• The inverse functions take a left-tail cumulative probability; an upper-tail percentage must first be converted (for example the top 5% means entering p = 0.95).

• EXPON.DIST(x, lambda, TRUE) gives the exponential cumulative probability.

Worked Examples

Standardizing a value: weekly sales

Weekly sales follow a normal distribution with mu = 100 and sigma = 25.

For a week with sales of 150: z = (150 - 100)/25 = 2.

Interpretation: sales of 150 sit exactly 2 standard deviations above the mean. Under the Empirical Rule, about 95% of weeks lie within 2 standard deviations, so a week at 150 is high but not extreme.

Type A: probabilities from a value (time on a website)

The time a visitor spends on a telecom company's website is normal with mu = 18 seconds and sigma = 5 seconds.

P(X < 18.6): NORM.DIST(18.6, 18, 5, TRUE) = 0.5478. The z route gives the same answer: z = (18.6 - 18)/5 = 0.12, and NORM.S.DIST(0.12, TRUE) = 0.5478.

P(X > 18.6) = 1 - 0.5478 = 0.4522, using the fact that the total area is 1.

P(18 < X < 18.6) = P(X < 18.6) - P(X < 18) = 0.5478 - 0.5 = 0.0478. The mean point must be computed explicitly as 0.5; the rule is always "upper bound minus lower bound".

P(17.4 < X < 18) = P(X < 18) - P(X < 17.4) = 0.5 - 0.4522 = 0.0478. Because 17.4 and 18.6 are equally far from the mean of 18, the two intervals must have the same probability, which is a good internal check.

Type B: a threshold from a probability (finding the bottom 20%)

For the same website times (mu = 18, sigma = 5), find the time x such that only 20% of visits are shorter, that is P(X < x) = 0.20.

Solve on the z scale first: NORM.S.INV(0.20) = z = -0.8416, about -0.84. The z is negative because 20% is below 50%.

Transform back: X = mu + Z sigma = 18 + (-0.84)(5) = 18 - 4.2 = 13.8 seconds.

Interpretation: about 20% of visitors, one in five, leave within about 13.8 seconds.

One-step Excel check: NORM.INV(0.2, 18, 5) gives the same 13.8.

Business meaning: a financial analyst estimates mu and sigma from history and then asks "below which return do my worst 10% of outcomes fall?" That is exactly the logic of risk tools such as Value at Risk. Every question of the form "what threshold is exceeded only by the top 5% (or the bottom 1%)" is this same calculation.

Normal probability from a mean and standard deviation

Monthly coffee spending is normal with mu = 30 dollars and sigma = 10 dollars. Find P(X < 50).

Standardize: z = (50 - 30)/10 = 2.

P(X < 50) = NORM.S.DIST(2, TRUE) = 0.9772, or directly NORM.DIST(50, 30, 10, TRUE).

Interpretation: about 97.7% of months have spending below 50 dollars; only about 2.3% exceed it.

Assessing normality on two data sets

• Data set 1: the skewness and kurtosis are clearly away from 0, the histogram is left-skewed with a sharp peak and heavy tails, the mean happens to be close to the median, and the IQR is smaller than 1.33 s. The checks disagree with a normal shape, so the data are not normal.

• Data set 2 (financial returns): the skewness and kurtosis are not exactly 0, but the mean is close to the median, the proportions within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations are close to 68%, 95% and 99.7%, and the IQR is close to 1.33 s. The checks are approximately satisfied, so a normal model is reasonable.

The lesson is that normality is a matter of approximation across several checks at once, not of one statistic being exactly right.

Uniform: how late is the bus?

A bus is defined as late when it leaves more than 2 minutes after the timetable, and lateness is uniformly distributed between 2 and 6 minutes: X ~ U(2, 6).

Density height: f(x) = 1/(B - A) = 1/(6 - 2) = 0.25 for 2 <= x <= 6.

Mean: mu = (2 + 6)/2 = 4 minutes.

Standard deviation: sigma = (6 - 2)/square root of 12 = 4/3.464 = 1.155 minutes.

P(3 <= X <= 5) = (5 - 3) x 0.25 = 0.5. Half of all late departures leave between 3 and 5 minutes after the timetable.

The probability of a departure delay exceeding 5.5 minutes is P(X > 5.5) = (6 - 5.5) x 0.25 = 0.125. Inferring a missed-connection probability would additionally require arrival delays, transfer time and the connecting timetable; departure lateness alone does not determine it.

Exponential: gaps between arrivals

Customers arrive at a service centre at 15 per hour. What is the probability that the gap between two consecutive arrivals is less than 3 minutes?

Match the units: the rate is 15 per hour, so the waiting time must be measured in hours. t = 3 minutes = 3/60 = 0.05 hours.

P(T < 0.05) = 1 - e^(-15 x 0.05) = 1 - e^(-0.75) = 1 - 0.4724 = 0.5276, about 52.8%.

Poisson cross-check: in 3 minutes the expected number of arrivals is lambda t = 15 x 0.05 = 0.75, and P(T > 0.05) = P(no arrivals in 3 minutes) = e^(-0.75) = 0.4724, which gives the same answer.

The mean gap is 1/lambda = 1/15 hour = 4 minutes.

Interpretation: more than half the time the next customer arrives within 3 minutes, even though the average gap is 4 minutes. Staffing should be built around this rhythm rather than around the naive assumption of one customer every 4 minutes.
